background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Well, short term, of course, is the COVID pandemic. We have to knock down these numbers to reopen our economy. The most important thing to fully reopen our economy is to knock down the COVID pandemic. The sooner we do that, the sooner we can fully reopen our economy. Now, we've done a good job in Washington in doing that. It's been very difficult, it's been very frustrating. We've had business losses that are hugely painful to me and everyone else for businesses that have not been able to weather this storm. But we have had relative success. Today, 45 other states have higher rates of infection than we do, which suggests we'll be able to get back sooner and better in our economic growth. So we are committed to that. We know that short term, there's things we need to do to help businesses. We've had a $25 million fund to help small businesses with grants to help them across. I look at this as we're all in a lifeboat. Waiting to get to the shore when we have a vaccine, frankly. So we wanna help businesses weather that storm. We've done some assistance to landlords, for instance, during this period of time. So those are the, COVID is the short term. Long term, we've gotta continue the tremendous work we've done in economic development. Now, it's hard to remember those brighter days of last year, but we had the best economy in the United States, or top one or two or three. That's why so many people are moving here to start businesses, to take high tech and other jobs. We've had fantastic success. And we ought to be proud of that. Business Insider Magazine listed us the best place to do business. CNBC said it was the best place to live. Oxfam said it's the best place to work. And this is pretty interesting. I don't know if any other state, simultaneously, has done this. It's been called the best place to do business and the best place to work. That's a pretty unusual twofer. And we've accomplished this because we've done some policies that recognize that reducing income inequality is a business growth strategy. Having adequately paid consumers or workers means we can have consumers to actually buy things. This is an economic growth strategy. And we've embedded that throughout our policies. That's why we've been very successful. So I'm actually very confident in our ability to come back better than any other state as soon as we get some better results on COVID. Now, we have all these other long-term things. Education. We've got to increase access not just to colleges but to technical careers. That's why I'm very excited about our apprenticeship program that is leading the nation and getting students into apprenticeships. Apprentices, apprenticeship opportunities. We want to sort of do what Switzerland does. About 70% of their students are in tech apprenticeship programs when they're in school. We want everybody to have a bright career. And we know we have a talent shortage for businesses in that regard. And not just when I say apprenticeships, people think immediately construction. And those are great apprenticeships. My son has been in one. But it's in health care. It's in advanced manufacturing. It's throughout our economy we can do this. Good for business, good for our students. We know we can grow clean energy jobs like crazy. And we're doing that. Our clean energy jobs are growing maybe three times faster than the rest of the economy. So there are a host of longer-term things we've got to do. Our transportation is going to need significant expansion. We don't know if that will be in the cards next session or not. We're talking to legislators about that right now. We need a big change. very robust capital budget so that we can build and we can put people to work this is the fastest way for economic infusion and i will be very aggressive trying to get the most ambitious capital budget we possibly can that's both good for you know building schools and building water systems we got to rebuild culverts as you know we're under an obligation to build culverts to restore fish runs this is a constitutional obligation in state of washington so i've mentioned a few of them but i got 100 in my back pocket but we only have 20 minutes

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: The assault weapon ban, so-called assault weapon ban on sales, it's come up, I think, six times since you've been in office. Hasn't passed. Democrats have a stronger majority this time around. Is this the year you saw the reaction yesterday, Republicans don't like the idea? Is this the year that that gets passed?

ground_truth: I think there's a good chance of that. Look, every time there's a shooting, every time we see our schoolchildren shot, I saw it at my old school that I went to, Ingraham High School, every time this is, people are now more willing that we have to act. Inaction is not acceptable to us against gun violence. So the assault weapon bill is just one of the things I think we need. I'm very committed to getting a bill through to say, look, you ought to have some basic safety training when you buy a gun. I think this is one of the very important things we need to do. Other states, Connecticut, have had success with these programs in reducing gun violence. I think we ought to do that. We expect you have some basic understanding of the safety protocols around guns. And responsible gun owners understand that. So I'm really going to push this bill this year. As you know, I've been a long supporter of the assault weapon ban. I actually provided one of the pivotal votes, one of the last votes in 1994, that passed it on a federal level, and it was successful while it was in operation for 10 years. Then the Republicans took it off the books, and look at the mass shootings we've had. So that's one of the three bills I think we need to get done.
